body:
Why different forms of protection are needed

Knowledge, skill and innovation create economic value in different ways. A handwoven textile may be valued because it comes from a particular region. A new crop variety may be valuable because it has improved characteristics. A manufacturing method may provide an advantage because competitors do not know it.

These situations involve different kinds of intellectual property protection. Geographical indications protect the connection between certain goods and their geographical origin. Plant variety protection recognises rights relating to eligible plant varieties while safeguarding important farmers' and researchers' interests. Trade secret protection concerns valuable information that is kept confidential.

The subject of protection matters

Geographical indications

Suppose buyers associate a particular textile with the traditional workmanship of a defined area. Its geographical identity and reputation may justify protection as a geographical indication. The central question is whether a quality, reputation or other characteristic of the goods is essentially attributable to their geographical origin.

Plant varieties

Suppose a breeder develops a crop variety with a useful and distinguishable characteristic. Protection may be available after registration under India's plant variety law, subject to the applicable requirements and exceptions. The protected subject is the variety, not every plant of that crop species.

Trade secrets

Suppose a manufacturer has a commercially useful preparation method known only to a restricted group of employees. The method may be protected as confidential know-how if it has the necessary secrecy and is properly safeguarded. Registration is not required, but the holder cannot prevent independent discovery or other lawful acquisition of the same information merely by claiming secrecy.

Public recognition and secrecy are different approaches

A geographical indication depends on establishing and communicating the relationship between goods and their origin. Plant variety registration involves identifying and describing a variety. A trade secret follows the opposite approach: its commercial advantage depends on preventing unauthorised disclosure.

These protections are not necessarily alternatives for an entire business. A textile enterprise may make goods associated with a registered geographical indication while separately protecting genuinely confidential business information. The rights must nevertheless be assessed independently; satisfying the conditions of one system does not automatically satisfy another.

Prelims focus

  • A geographical indication concerns goods linked to a geographical area.
  • Plant variety protection concerns eligible varieties registered under a specific Indian law.
  • A trade secret concerns commercially valuable confidential information.
  • GI registration and plant variety registration are different from maintaining a trade secret.
  • Trap: A valuable product, a valuable plant variety and valuable confidential information do not receive identical legal protection.

[Sources: Intellectual Property India, Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act, 1999, section 2; India Code, Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers' Rights Act, 2001, preamble and sections 14–15; World Intellectual Property Organization, Trade Secrets, sections 'What is a trade secret?' and 'What kind of information is protected?', consulted 14 November 2026; NCERT, Living Craft Traditions of India, Class 11, chapter 'Crafts Heritage', printed pp. 9–13.]

title: Understanding Intellectual Property: Origin, Plant Varieties and Confidential Knowledge

body:
Meaning of a geographical indication

A geographical indication (GI) identifies goods as originating in a country, region or locality where a given quality, reputation or other characteristic of those goods is essentially attributable to their geographical origin.

A GI therefore communicates more than an address. It connects particular goods with a geographical area and with a characteristic or reputation associated with that area. The required connection may arise from natural conditions, human skills and traditions, or a combination of these factors.

How geography influences goods

Natural factors

Climate, soil, local environmental conditions and other natural features may influence agricultural or natural products. When such factors are important to the recognised characteristics of goods, they can help establish their geographical connection.

Human factors

Traditional weaving, embroidery, dyeing, carving and other specialised skills may give handicrafts a recognised regional character. Techniques transmitted across generations can become closely associated with a particular locality.

For example, Patan Patola is associated with the traditional textile workmanship of Patan in Gujarat. Its identity involves inherited craft knowledge as well as geographical association. A GI identifies goods meeting the applicable geographical and product requirements; it does not confer ownership of the underlying craft skill on one individual.

Which goods may receive GI protection?

India's Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act, 1999 covers agricultural goods, natural goods and manufactured goods, including handicrafts, industrial goods and foodstuffs.

For manufactured goods, the statutory definition also requires that at least one activity of production, processing or preparation take place in the relevant geographical area. The precise registered description and geographical boundaries determine the scope of a particular GI.

Quality, reputation or another characteristic can establish the geographical connection. The law does not require every GI product to possess all 3 simultaneously.

GI is different from an ordinary place-of-manufacture label

A statement that a shirt was manufactured in a certain city may simply identify where it was made. That statement alone does not establish that the shirt has a recognised characteristic or reputation essentially attributable to that place. The geographical connection required for a GI must be supported by evidence.

Similarly, a producer cannot obtain GI protection simply by adding the name of a famous town to unrelated goods. The indication must concern qualifying goods and a defined geographical area.

GI and trademark: an important distinction

FeatureGeographical indicationTrademark
Main purposeIdentifies qualifying goods by geographical originDistinguishes the goods or services of one business from those of others
Underlying connectionGoods, place and associated quality, reputation or characteristicCommercial source or brand identity
UseAvailable to registered authorised users satisfying the applicable conditionsControlled by the trademark proprietor, subject to trademark law
Subject matterGoodsGoods and services

A GI is thus generally a collective geographical identifier rather than the private brand name of a single manufacturer. It may coexist with trademarks on the same product, but each performs a different legal function.

What cannot be registered?

Section 9 of the GI Act excludes indications that are deceptive, contrary to law, scandalous or obscene, likely to hurt religious susceptibilities, or otherwise disentitled to protection in a court. It also excludes generic names: names that have lost their original geographical meaning and become common names for a kind of product. A name that misleadingly suggests another geographical origin can also be refused.

Prelims focus

  • India's principal GI legislation is the Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act, 1999.
  • Section 2 links qualifying goods with geographical origin and an attributable quality, reputation or other characteristic.
  • GI protection covers goods, including agricultural goods and handicrafts, rather than services.
  • For manufactured goods, at least one of production, processing or preparation must occur in the relevant area.
  • Section 9 prohibits registration of certain indications, including generic names.
  • Trap: Mere manufacture in a place does not automatically make a product eligible for GI registration.

[Sources: Intellectual Property India, Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act, 1999, sections 2, 8–9; Intellectual Property India, Geographical Indications: An Introduction, sections on meaning, eligible goods and prohibited indications, consulted 14 November 2026; NCERT, Living Craft Traditions of India, Class 11, 'Crafts Heritage', printed pp. 9–13.]

title: Geographical Indications: The Relationship Between Goods and Place

body:
The Indian legal and administrative framework

The Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act, 1999 came into force on 15 September 2003. The Geographical Indications Registry was established at Chennai on the same date, with all-India jurisdiction. The Controller General of Patents, Designs and Trade Marks functions as the Registrar of Geographical Indications.

Who applies to register a GI?

Under section 11, an association of persons or producers, an organisation, or an authority established under law may apply if it represents the interests of producers of the goods concerned. The applicant seeks registration for the geographical indication associated with specified goods and a defined area.

A proper application contains evidence of the connection between the goods and their geographical origin. It also identifies the category of goods, the geographical area and relevant characteristics. A geographical map forms part of the statutory application requirements.

How registration takes place

  1. Application: An eligible body applies to the GI Registrar with the required particulars and fee.
  2. Examination: The Registrar assesses the application and may accept it, impose conditions or refuse it.
  3. Publication: An accepted application is advertised so that objections may be raised.
  4. Opposition: Any person may oppose within 3 months of advertisement, extendable by the Registrar by up to 1 month; the applicant must file a counter-statement within 2 months of receiving the notice or the application is deemed abandoned, and the Registrar decides after considering the evidence and hearing the parties if requested.
  5. Registration: If the application is accepted and no successful opposition prevents registration, the indication is entered in the register and a certificate is issued.

Registered proprietor and authorised user are not the same

The registered proprietor is the association or other eligible body recorded as proprietor of the GI. An authorised user is a person claiming to be a producer of the relevant goods who obtains registration to use the registered indication.

Under section 21, both the registered proprietor and authorised users can obtain relief for infringement. However, the exclusive right to use the GI in relation to the registered goods is specifically conferred on authorised users, subject to the conditions and limitations of registration. More than one qualifying producer can become an authorised user.

Registration of the GI identifies and protects the geographical indication. Registration as an authorised user establishes a qualifying producer's right to use that registered indication. The 2 registrations serve different purposes.

Validity and renewal

A GI registration lasts for 10 years and can be renewed for further 10-year periods. An authorised user's registration lasts for 10 years or until the underlying GI registration expires, whichever is earlier, subject to the statutory renewal provisions. Failure to renew can lead to removal from the register.

What amounts to infringement?

Section 22 covers unauthorised use that misleads people about the geographical origin of registered goods. It also addresses specified forms of unfair competition and misleading representations. For example, describing goods made outside the qualifying area as genuine goods of a protected geographical origin may constitute infringement.

Registration helps the proprietor and authorised users enforce the GI through legal proceedings. Under section 67, civil remedies can include an injunction, which orders a party to stop specified conduct, and, subject to the court's decision, damages or an account of profits. An account of profits concerns profits attributable to the wrongful activity rather than ordinary compensation for the claimant's loss.

GI registration is not compulsory. However, section 20 prevents a statutory infringement action for an unregistered GI while preserving the separate legal remedy of passing off, which addresses a misleading representation that one's goods are those of another person or have a false commercial association.

Can a registered GI be sold or licensed?

Section 24 generally prohibits assignment, transmission, licensing, pledging or mortgaging of rights in a registered GI. This reflects its connection to a geographical community rather than ownership by one freely transferable business. The Act contains a specific exception allowing an authorised user's right to devolve on a successor in title upon the user's death.

This does not prevent the ordinary lawful resale of genuine GI goods. Section 22 also recognises that further dealings in lawfully acquired goods do not ordinarily constitute GI infringement, subject to the qualification concerning impairment of their condition.

Prelims focus

  • The GI Act was enacted in 1999 and came into force on 15 September 2003.
  • The GI Registry is headquartered in Chennai.
  • Section 11 concerns applications for GI registration; section 17 concerns authorised users.
  • Section 18 provides a 10-year registration period and renewal.
  • Section 21 distinguishes the proprietor's enforcement right from an authorised user's right to use the GI.
  • Trap: A registered GI cannot ordinarily be assigned or licensed like an individual business asset.

[Sources: Government of India, Gazette notifications S.O. 1051(E) and S.O. 1052(E), dated 15 September 2003; Intellectual Property India, Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act, 1999, sections 3, 11–18, 20–24 and 66–67; Intellectual Property India, Geographical Indications: An Introduction, sections on application, authorised users and renewal, consulted 14 November 2026.]
